sources: Lahore: A Framework for Urban Conservation (Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme, 2019)

landmarks.name: Sheesh Mahal
landmarks.description: One of the most celebrated monuments in Lahore Fort, the Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) was built by Shah Jahan as part of the Shah Burj complex. Its facade consists of five multi-cusped marble arches supported by coupled columns. The interior walls and ceilings are encrusted with intricate mirror and coloured-glass mosaic work (kund-kari), reflecting candlelight to create a dazzling effect.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — UNESCO World Heritage Site component

landmarks.name: Alamgiri Gate
landmarks.description: The main western entrance gate to Lahore Fort, built by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1673. The gate faces the Badshahi Mosque across the Hazuri Bagh. It is a monumental structure flanked by two large semi-circular bastions decorated with white marble and faience tile-work. The gate served as the ceremonial royal entrance during the Mughal period.
landmarks.significance: High — primary Fort entrance, faces Badshahi Mosque
landmarks.status: Open to visitors — main entry point

landmarks.name: Akbari Gate
landmarks.description: The Akbari Gate is the oldest surviving gate of Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Akbar as part of his early fortification programme. It connects the Diwan-i-Amm quadrangle to the eastern sector of the Fort. The gate reflects Akbar's early architectural style, blending Timurid Central Asian forms with Indian craftsmanship.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — oldest surviving gate in the Fort

landmarks.name: Arz Gah
landmarks.description: The Arz Gah (Hall of Petitions) was the formal space within Lahore Fort where petitioners and visiting dignitaries presented their cases and gifts to the Mughal emperor. Located adjacent to the Diwan-i-Amm, it served as an antechamber to the main audience hall. The space reflects the highly regulated protocol of the Mughal court, where access to the emperor was carefully managed through a series of formal stages.
landmarks.significance: Medium — important administrative space of the Mughal court

landmarks.name: Barood Khana
landmarks.description: The Barood Khana (Gunpowder House) was the imperial armoury and ammunition depot of Lahore Fort, used to store gunpowder, weapons, and military supplies for the garrison. Its thick-walled, vaulted construction was designed to contain accidental explosions and protect the contents from fire. During the Sikh and British periods, it continued to serve military storage functions. It stands as evidence of the Fort's dual role as both a royal residence and a military stronghold.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving Mughal military-industrial structure

landmarks.name: Diwan-i-Amm
landmarks.description: The Diwan-i-Amm (Hall of Public Audience) is where the Mughal emperors held public court sessions to hear petitions from ordinary citizens. The structure is a colonnaded hall facing an open quadrangle, used by Shah Jahan and successive emperors to dispense justice and receive public delegations. A raised marble platform at the rear marks where the imperial throne once stood.

landmarks.name: Doulat Khana
landmarks.description: The Doulat Khana (House of Wealth or Treasury) forms the northern arcade of Jahangir's Quadrangle and was one of the most important residential and administrative buildings of Lahore Fort. It served as the private imperial apartments where the emperor held intimate meetings with senior courtiers. The facade of the Doulat Khana is a masterpiece of early Mughal architecture, featuring elegant multi-cusped arches and refined stonework that predates Shah Jahan's later marble embellishments.
landmarks.significance: High — central residential complex of Jahangir's Fort; masterpiece of early Mughal architecture

landmarks.name: Hathi Paer Stairs
landmarks.description: Hathi Paer Stairs — literally 'Elephant Feet Stairs' — are the broad, gently inclined ramps built within Lahore Fort to allow war elephants and mounted cavalry to access the upper levels of the Fort complex. Unlike conventional human staircases, these wide sloping passages were engineered to bear the enormous weight of royal elephants used in ceremonial processions and military displays. They are a remarkable example of Mughal military-architectural engineering.
landmarks.significance: High — unique Mughal military engineering; elephant ramps are rare surviving examples

landmarks.name: Haveli Mai Jindan
landmarks.description: Haveli Mai Jindan is the residential quarters associated with Rani Jindan (Mai Jindan), the youngest wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and mother of the last Sikh ruler Maharaja Duleep Singh. She was one of the most politically significant women of the Sikh Empire, serving as regent after Ranjit Singh's death in 1839. The haveli represents the Sikh period's residential architectural tradition within the Fort, blending Mughal spatial organisation with Sikh decorative sensibilities.
landmarks.significance: High — rare Sikh-period residential structure; associated with a major historical figure

landmarks.name: Jahangir's Quadrangle
landmarks.description: The largest quadrangle within Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Jahangir. The courtyard was recently restored with its historical water features and pools reinstated. The four sides of the quadrangle are lined with elegant arcaded halls. The northern facade, known as the Daulat Khana-e-Khaas-o-Aam, is a masterpiece of early Mughal architecture. The quadrangle served as the imperial residential and administrative core of the Fort.
landmarks.significance: High — central Mughal residential complex; recently restored

landmarks.name: Lal Burj
landmarks.description: Lal Burj (Red Tower) is one of the defensive bastions of Lahore Fort, named for its characteristic red brick construction. Located at a corner of the Fort's defensive perimeter, it originally served as a military watchtower and cannon platform. The use of red brick (as opposed to the white marble of Shah Jahan's period) indicates its construction during the earlier Akbari or Jahangiri phase of the Fort's development, when brick and sandstone were the primary materials.
landmarks.significance: Medium — early Mughal defensive architecture; contrasts with later marble constructions

landmarks.name: Maktab Khana
landmarks.description: The Maktab Khana (Royal School or Scriptorium) was the imperial space within Lahore Fort designated for learning, manuscript copying, and royal correspondence. Mughal emperors placed great value on education and literary culture — Jahangir and Shah Jahan both maintained extensive court libraries. The Maktab Khana served as both an administrative writing office and a place of formal instruction for princes of the royal household.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving educational structure within a Mughal fort

landmarks.name: Moti Masjid
landmarks.description: The Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) is a small but elegant private mosque built within Lahore Fort for the imperial family's personal prayers. Constructed of white marble, it features three domed bays and a rectangular prayer chamber. The mosque is notable for its fine proportions and purity of white marble. Similar mosques of the same name exist in Delhi's Red Fort and Agra Fort, reflecting Shah Jahan's characteristic architectural language.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — example of imperial private mosque architecture

landmarks.name: Picture Wall
landmarks.description: The Picture Wall is a 1,450-foot-long exterior wall running along the northern and western faces of Lahore Fort. Built during the reign of Emperor Jahangir, it is decorated with elaborate glazed-tile mosaic work (kashi-kari) depicting hunting scenes, combat between mythological animals, polo matches, portraits of courtiers, and geometric patterns. It is considered one of the largest examples of Mughal decorative tile-work in existence.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — largest Mughal tile-work panel in existence

landmarks.name: Royal Kitchen
landmarks.description: The Royal Kitchen (Shahi Bawarchi Khana) is a large complex of vaulted service buildings in the south-western part of Lahore Fort that once served the royal household. The kitchens are notable for their massive chimneys, ventilation shafts, and storage chambers designed to support large-scale food preparation for the imperial court. They are currently being adapted for reuse as a museum and visitor facility as part of the AKTC/WCLA conservation programme.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving service complex; being adaptively reused

landmarks.name: Shah Jahan Quadrangle
landmarks.description: The Shah Jahan Quadrangle is one of the principal open courts within Lahore Fort, developed during the reign of Emperor Shah Jahan. The quadrangle is flanked by arcaded halls and residential chambers that once housed the emperor's private quarters (Khwabgah). Shah Jahan's architectural vision — characterised by white marble, intricate inlay, and formal garden layouts — is expressed throughout this section of the Fort.
landmarks.significance: High — central to Shah Jahan's Fort expansion; links to Khwabgah and Sheesh Mahal
